final_answer: BLOCKED ON VERIFICATION: every primary-source fetch (law.lis.virginia.gov, vacode.org, Cornell, Justia) was refused by the network egress proxy, so no authority passed the citation firewall and none is cited. The following is an unverified, from-memory analysis, to be confirmed against the Code of Virginia, Title 8.2A. Likely bottom line: No, Client probably cannot stop paying, and Lessor is probably not responsible for the defective Trailers. Reasoning: (1) Virginia Article 2A (Va. Code 8.2A-101 et seq.) governs the lease of goods. (2) The facts fit a 'finance lease' under 8.2A-103(1)(g): Lessor did not select, manufacture or supply the goods, acquired them in connection with the lease, and Client received a copy of the supply contract (including the warranty) before signing; Client, not Lessor, chose the model and negotiated specs with Manufacturer. (3) In a finance lease that is not a consumer lease (Client is a business), 8.2A-407 makes the lessee's promises irrevocable and independent upon acceptance, and a 'hell or high water' clause like this one is enforceable; the lessee cannot withhold rent over goods defects. (4) The finance lessor gives no implied warranties of merchantability or fitness (8.2A-212, 213 apply to non-finance leases), and under 8.2A-209 the lessee instead receives the benefit of the supplier's promises and warranties, so Client's remedy is against Manufacturer (here, a proof of claim in the Chapter 7, with likely little recovery). (5) Lessor is not liable unless it made its own promises or misrepresentations, the Lease was not a true finance lease, or there is fraud/bad faith; none appear in the facts. Other points to check: whether Client formally accepted the goods (8.2A-515/516) and whether revocation of acceptance is available against Lessor (finance-lease limits, 8.2A-517); Lessor's remedies on default (8.2A-523 et seq.), acceleration and damages exposure; and whether the Lease provides for a security interest or purchase option. Client should keep paying or negotiate with Lessor; stopping payments exposes it to default remedies.
